coherence.reasons: Both run a clean line from a quantified bridge to sized levers, a total and a sequence. X's summary maps one-to-one onto its sections and its governing thought honestly says "close to 3.0%". But X has two internal tensions. It argues each 1% fewer hours adds about 0.08 pp of shrink, yet its base case quietly needs about 3.8% fewer hours per sales dollar to absorb the 2027 wage rise, with no shrink penalty. It also headlines that the first two actions "can clear the FY2026 covenant" and then concedes most of FY2026 may have passed. Y carries the wage headwind and the targeted hours trim as explicit bridge lines, and its waves reconcile to the total (23.2 after Wave 1; 6.3, 7.1 and 7.3 later). Y's flaw is small: one-time cost is about $18M on one page but the wave costs sum to about $19.5M, with $1.5M of three-store closing cost dropped.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the 8% cut, reprice delivery rather than freeze or kill it, prune losing promotions away from ValuMart, and exit stores at lease expiry. Y weighs the trade-offs more defensibly. It sizes promotion pruning to 25% with a 30% volume give-back, where X assumes a full return to 24% with zero lost volume despite calling ValuMart traffic the largest risk. Y puts the $6.8M wage rise in the base case; X leaves it out and shows it only as a sensitivity that drops the plan to about 2.5%. Y budgets realistic one-time costs (about $18M) against X's $7.5M, which assumes shrink, scheduling and private-label work cost nothing. Y also names about $10M of contingency levers, sets trigger-and-response rules per risk, proposes a fix-or-exit gate for the three long-lease stores, and treats the covenant realistically with a lender briefing and possible waiver. X has good elements: a sensitivity table, a list of rejected routes and treating the delivery re-tender as part of the plan. But its base case is more fragile and its covenant answer depends on a start date that may have passed. Y's simultaneous 3% net hours cut and shrink fall to 2.3% is optimistic, but it is flagged and has a trigger.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the required numbers accurately: the bridge (e-commerce −12.6, promotions −10.5, shrink −7.5, labor −4.5), the −$10.4M e-commerce drag, −$12.34 and −$1.64 per order, the $2.8M fee rollout, $6.6M from closures and the roughly $30M gap. Both debunk the 6.1% claim and the category team's correlation with a break-even test. X stays closer to the pack: it rebuilds the $18.1M fulfillment line from order data, sizes shrink conservatively (Q1 and Q2 to the Q3 level, $3.5M), extrapolates private label at the historical pace, and notes where its e-commerce estimate is favourable. Its weak spots are the zero-give-back promotion lever and the uncosted wage absorption. Y introduces more figures the pack does not support: a vendor-funding lever resting on an inferred $113M markdown base and a contestable reading of the 14-pt gap, a 30% give-back, private label accelerating to 1 pt a year, chain shrink reaching the best-quartile level while hours fall, and several cost allowances. All are flagged, but they carry about a third of Y's plan value. Y's explanation of why labor looks like the cause (+$14.3M in dollars, the largest cost rise) is a good use of evidence.

revision.reasons: Both revise the wage hypothesis firmly and on the right grounds: labor is about 13% of the decline, the 9.4% wage rise was mostly offset by 6% fewer hours per sales dollar, and the low-labor quartile has the highest shrink. Both estimate that the 8% cut could give back about $10M and label that an upper bound or association. Both reject the e-commerce freeze as locking in a roughly $10M loss. X gives wages a dedicated page and a backup on absorbing the 2027 rise. Y explains why management's view is understandable and values the draft plan net of the 2027 wage rise (0.8%–1.5%). Both keep a targeted labor-productivity element rather than discarding labor entirely. The differences are negligible.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, correctly diagnosed, fully sized plans that land near 3.0% and replace the management draft. X is the more rigorous evidence audit and is more conservative about inventing inputs. Y is the better decision document for the CEO and board. Its base case already absorbs the 2027 wage rise and promotional volume loss. It budgets one-time cost realistically inside the $25M and names contingency levers for a thin base case. It sets triggers and pre-agreed responses, frames four explicit board decisions, and is realistic that FY2026 is largely set, so the lender needs a briefing. X's headline 2.97% depends on an unpriced wage absorption and a full, loss-free promotion reset, so its plan is less robust than it looks, though it discloses this in sensitivities. Y's extra assumptions (vendor funding, allowances) are a real weakness but are flagged and partly held as contingency.
